title: The MEGA Fork
reviewNotes: All 30 saved images and narration re-reviewed, with the complete native post-fork diagram checked. The seven-piece start after ...e3 is explicitly reconstructed across the 89–90 second a7/e4 to Qa8/e3 transition. Two branches verify a8=Q/e2/Qa6+/Kd5/Qxe2 and an independent rook underpromotion that draws. The earlier eleven-piece queen sacrifice and knight forks remain unverified source context; the small later conversion does not certify them.
transcript: White's brilliant idea is knight to c6, check, now forking the king and the queen. But of course this seems to be a blunder because the knight can simply be captured by the black rook. And now not only white is losing, but it's completely lost, having only a knight against a rook and bishop. But you see white had foreseen a brilliant sequence that relies on sacrificing almost every single one of his pieces to win this game. And the game for black is completely lost after the beautiful and majestic queen to f5, check. A beautiful sacrifice that has to be accepted because if the king moves, now white is going to pick up the black queen. And after we lose the knight, we're going to get a second queen, and this is completely winning for white. But after the black king takes this queen, it now seems like black is completely out of the woods. He has a queen, a rook, and a bishop for only one knight and pawn. But here comes the wake-up call. Knight to d4, check, forking the king and rook. And this might seem like not the end of the world. Even if black loses the rook, he's still going to have an entire queen. But that is not the case because this black king cannot move anywhere except for e5, which means that on the next move white is going to take the rook with a check and a fork, allowing white to win the queen. And incredibly, even if black has one bishop left, there is no way to prevent the promotion to a new queen. So white will get the queen, stop the pawn, and win the game. If you love majestic chess, follow me for more.
